parts.title: A night at the museum
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last month, my class spent the night in our city's natural history museum. We arrived at six o'clock with sleeping bags, and our teacher told us the rules: no running, no shouting and absolutely no touching the exhibits. At first, the huge rooms seemed very quiet and slightly scary.

After a pizza dinner, we went on a torch tour. The guide, a tall man called Gareth, showed us the skeleton of a giant whale that hangs from the ceiling. He told us that when the museum was new, people believed that the bones belonged to a sea monster. Everyone laughed.

We slept on the floor in the room with the stuffed animals. I could not fall asleep for a long time, because I kept imagining that the wolf in the corner was moving. At about midnight, somebody's alarm clock rang, and half the class screamed.

In the morning, we were tired but happy. The museum gave each of us a small badge, and I have pinned mine to my school bag. I would definitely do it again, but next time I would bring earplugs.

questions.prompt: What was one of the rules?
options: No sleeping bags in the halls
No talking at all during dinner
questions.explanation: The teacher said absolutely no touching the exhibits.

options: They had been found in a lake
They were only a few years old
They were hung by a king
questions.explanation: He said people believed the bones belonged to a sea monster.

options: The floor felt very hard and cold

questions.explanation: She kept imagining that the wolf in the corner was moving.

parts.title: The history of museums
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
The word museum comes from ancient Greece, where it meant a place for the Muses, the goddesses of art and science. [1] However, these were not like the museums that we visit today.

Many early collections belonged to rich families. [2] Ordinary people could only see them if they knew the owners.

In the eighteenth century, some collections were opened to everyone. [3] Visitors could walk round for free, although they sometimes had to book weeks in advance.

By the nineteenth century, most large cities had their own museum. [4] Schools began to organise trips, and soon children were an important part of the audience.

Today, museums try to make visits more exciting. [5] Many have films, games and quizzes, so that visitors of all ages can learn while they enjoy themselves.
sentences: They filled their houses with paintings, fossils and rare objects.
They were now seen as places for learning, not only for the rich.
This was a big change, because before then only a few people could enter.
Some museums do not have any visitors at all.
The oldest one in Britain opened in Oxford in 1683.
Some of the first collections were kept in temples.
That is still true in some small towns today.
They also know that visitors like to take part.

gaps.explanation: The first collections were in temples; the next sentence says they were not like museums today.
Rich families filled their houses with objects, and ordinary people could only see them if they knew the owners.
Opening collections to everyone was a big change; the next sentence says visitors could walk round for free.
Museums were seen as places for learning; the next sentence says schools organised trips.
Visitors like to take part; the next sentence lists films, games and quizzes.

From one picture to another is a fixed pattern.

parts.title: A tour of the City History Museum
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Good morning, and welcome to the City History Museum. My name is Ove, and I will be your guide today. The tour lasts one hour and fifteen minutes. Last month it was one hour and a half, but visitors told us that was too long, so we cut a room. We’ll start on the ground floor. Many people ask me if this building was a school or a hospital, because it looks like one. In fact, it was a prison until nineteen fifty, and the thick walls and small windows are still here. Please look at the door on your left. It’s the original one. Let’s move on to the first room, where we keep the oldest things in the collection. Look at the glass case. People expect a coin or a bowl, but our oldest object is a clay pot, almost three thousand years old. It was found by children in a field. Now, in the next room, there are screens and buttons. If you press the red button, you can hear a story. The green button is the one that plays the sounds from the past, such as horses, bells and voices in the street. Please be gentle, they are sensitive. After that, we’ll climb to the first floor, where our special exhibition is. It is about the old market, which stood in front of the museum for five hundred years. The exhibition about the harbour was last year, and it’s finished. You’ll see photos, scales and even a market stall that you can touch. At the end of the tour, you can have a drink in the café. Show your ticket at the till, and you’ll get ten per cent off. Students get twenty per cent in the shop, but only on Wednesdays. Any questions before we begin?

gaps.explanation: The tour lasts one hour and fifteen minutes; one and a half hours was last month’s tour.

gaps.prompt: Before it became a museum, the building was a ___
gaps.explanation: It looks like a school or hospital, but it was a prison until nineteen fifty.

gaps.prompt: The oldest object in the collection is a clay ___
gaps.explanation: People expect a coin or a bowl, but the oldest object is a clay pot.

gaps.prompt: To listen to sounds from the past, press the ___ button
gaps.explanation: The red button plays a story and the green button plays the sounds.

gaps.prompt: The special exhibition is about the old ___
gaps.explanation: The exhibition is about the old market; the harbour exhibition was last year.

gaps.prompt: With your ticket, the café gives ___ per cent off
gaps.explanation: The café gives ten per cent off; twenty per cent is the student discount in the shop.

parts.title: An interview with a museum curator
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Maddox, many people don’t know what a curator does. What is your job?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: I get that all the time. I don’t sell tickets, that’s the front desk, and I don’t clean the halls, we have a lovely team for that. My job is to look after the objects: to choose them, record them and keep them safe for the future. I know each one like a friend. Some of them have been in the museum for a hundred years, and I even talk to them when nobody is around. My colleagues find that funny.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: You have a pair of paper shoes in the collection. Why were they made?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: They’re fascinating. Some people think it was a joke, and in a way they are funny, but no. A film company didn’t ask for them either. They were made in 1932 by a dancer who couldn’t afford leather. She had no money, so she used newspaper and glue, and she still danced in them. They survived because her daughter kept them in a box in the attic, and later gave them to us.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What damages old objects?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Dust is a nuisance, but you can clean it, and the roof is fine, we fixed the leak years ago. The real enemies are light and heat. They make colours fade and paper turn yellow. That’s why some rooms are so dark, and that is why I’m always arguing with visitors who want more lights!

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do visitors often get wrong?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Many people think that museums are boring, and that’s changing slowly. They also think tickets are free, but only on certain days. The biggest mistake is believing that everything is on display. In fact, ninety per cent of our collection is in storage, because there isn’t enough room. We change the display every few months, so even regular visitors will always find something new when they come back.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: How did you become a curator?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: I didn’t win a prize, and I never worked in a shop. I studied history at university, and then I volunteered here on Saturdays for three years, cleaning labels and carrying boxes. When a job opened, they remembered me. I was so nervous at the interview that I forgot my own name for a second, but they gave me the job anyway.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What advice do you give to young people?

turns.speaker: h
turns.text: Ask questions, always. When you stand in front of an object and wonder who made it, you start to find the story. You don’t have to study art, and you don’t have to travel. Just be curious, because every discovery begins with a question.
